Q: How to copy Associative Array without for loop A:

I know the topic is a bit older, but after looking into this, here's a solution that should work better than messing with strings by using Bash's "parameter operator" from 3.5.3 Shell Parameter Expansion right at the bottom.

Everything you see here is done on GNU bash, Version 5.3.9(1)-release .

The trick is to know how to write the declaration. It is important to quote the full statement when copying the arrays, so instead of

declare -A a="(${a[@]@K})"

or

declare -A a=("${a[@]@K}")

you need to write

declare -A "a=(${a[@]@K})"

while using the "@K" operator (capital "K").

The manual says:

"K"

Produces a possibly-quoted version of the value of parameter, except that it prints the values of indexed and associative arrays as a sequence of quoted key-value pairs (see Arrays). The keys and values are quoted in a format that can be reused as input.

Let's declare two associative arrays:

declare -A a=("a b c" "1 2 3" "d e f" "4 5 6")
declare -A b=([g h i]="7 8 9" ["j k l"]="10 11 12")

The "K" operator gives you the key/value pairs enclosed in quotes as a single string, like so:

$ for i in "${a[@]@K}"; do echo ">${i}<"; done
>"d e f" "4 5 6" "a b c" "1 2 3" <

I added the "><" to make this visible. Instead of getting four values for "${i}", two keys and two values, you get one single string which is a bit irritating at first and why you need to quote the full declaration.

Let's copy the arrays "a,b" to "c,d":

declare -A "c=(${a[@]@K})"
declare -A "d=(${b[@]@K})"

And you will get:

$ declare -p c d
declare -A c=(["d e f"]="4 5 6" ["a b c"]="1 2 3" )
declare -A d=(["g h i"]="7 8 9" ["j k l"]="10 11 12" )

There are multiple ways to add one array to another:

On definition:

$ declare -A "c=(${a[@]@K}${b[@]@K})"
$ declare -p c
declare -A c=(["d e f"]="4 5 6" ["a b c"]="1 2 3" ["g h i"]="7 8 9" ["j k l"]="10 11 12" )

Or via "+=" operator:

$ declare -A "c=(${a[@]@K})"
$ declare "c+=(${b[@]@K})"

You can also use eval

$  eval "c+=(${b[@]@K})"

Result in both cases:

$ declare -p c
declare -A c=(["d e f"]="4 5 6" ["a b c"]="1 2 3" ["g h i"]="7 8 9" ["j k l"]="10 11 12" )

If you add an array that contains keys that already exist, then the shell replaces the values:

$ declare -A a=("a b c" "1 2 3" "d e f" "4 5 6")
$ declare -A b=([a b c]="7 8 9" ["d e f"]="10 11 12")
$ declare -p a b
declare -A a=(["d e f"]="4 5 6" ["a b c"]="1 2 3" )
declare -A b=(["d e f"]="10 11 12" ["a b c"]="7 8 9" )

Now add both to "c":

$ echo "c=(${a[@]@K}${b[@]@K})"
c=("d e f" "4 5 6" "a b c" "1 2 3" "d e f" "10 11 12" "a b c" "7 8 9" )

$ declare -A "c=(${a[@]@K}${b[@]@K})"
$ declare -p c
declare -A c=(["d e f"]="10 11 12" ["a b c"]="7 8 9" )

And via addition assignment operator ("+="):

$ unset c
$ declare -A "c=(${a[@]@K})"
$ declare -p c
declare -A c=(["d e f"]="4 5 6" ["a b c"]="1 2 3" )

$ declare -A "c+=(${b[@]@K})"
$ declare -p c
declare -A c=(["d e f"]="10 11 12" ["a b c"]="7 8 9" )
